The Columbia River. The longest river in the Pacific Northwest, the Columbia flows approximately one thousand two hundred forty miles from British Columbia through Washington and Oregon to the Pacific Ocean. It is a defining geographical feature of the Pacific Northwest and one of North America's most powerful rivers, generating enormous hydroelectric power and historically supporting a rich salmon fishery. The river originates in the Canadian Rockies near Columbia Lake in British Columbia and flows south and west into the United States. It forms the natural boundary between Washington and Oregon for much of its course. Extensive damming by the Grand Coulee Dam and other major hydroelectric projects has created a cascade of reservoirs that transformed the region's landscape and ecology. American fur traders named it after the Columbia, a merchant ship that explored its mouth in the late eighteenth century. Once it supported one of the world's richest salmon fisheries, but dam construction severely depleted salmon populations by blocking their migration routes. The river was used by Lewis and Clark as a crucial part of their expedition route to reach the Pacific Ocean from eighteen hundred five to eighteen hundred six. The Columbia discharges more water into the Pacific Ocean than any other North American river, sharing this distinction with its largest tributary, the Snake River.
